newsitem.title: USA: AT&T results skid; in line with lowered expectations.
newsitem.headline: AT&T results skid; in line with lowered expectations.

text.p: AT&T Corp., which last week shocked Wall Street by announcing that its chairman-in-waiting had resigned under pressure, Monday reported a 36 percent decline in profits for the second quarter.
The nation's biggest long-distance phone company said it earned $959 million in the quarter, down from $1.5 billion a year earlier, as investments in new markets trimmed results.
The profits equalled 59 cents a share, down from 92 cents a share a year earlier. Sales rose to $13.2 billion from $12.9 billion.

The results met Wall Street's expectations that the company would earn 58 cents a share, according to estimates compiled by First Call. AT&T stock fell 12.5 cents to $34.25 in composite New York Stock Exchange trading.

"While we are making good progress against the commitments we made to our investors earlier this year, we're certainly not pleased with the year-over-year decline in our earnings," Chairman Robert Allen said. "Our results reflect the short-term effect of our strategy to strengthen and grow the business over the long term."

AT&T Chief Financial Officer Dan Somers said that earnings comparisons should become more favourable in future quarters. In a conference call with analysts and reporters, he said he was confident the company could meet Wall Street's third quarter average estimate of 64 cents a share.

AT&T shocked the industry and Wall Street on Wednesday when John Walter, handpicked last November to succeed Allen, suddenly resigned. The company's board said it would not promote him to chief executive in January, as originally planned, because it had decided he was not suited to the job.

AT&T said profits were reduced by its investments in wireless and local phone service and the Internet. Sales growth was driven by business long-distance services, wireless services and AT&T Solutions, its systems integration business. Financial services revenue declined.

Revenue growth lagged the 8 percent growth seen at rival Sprint Corp., and the 4 percent to 5 percent growth expected from MCI Communications Corp., the No. 2 long-distance company. That translates into further market share losses for AT&T, which serves about 80 million residential customers and 10 million business customers.
Analysts said there were few surprises in the report that would lead them to revise their opinions on AT&T's lagging stock.
"They came in slightly ahead of anticipated," CS First Boston analyst Frank Governali said. "But there is nothing here that should cause a major change in the view of their prospects."
Revenues were pressured by new business contracts, changes in product mix, the use of free calling minutes and increased customer acceptance of calling plans, the company said.

Allen said the company remains committed to delivering on its overall financial targets, "despite the fact that our local service efforts have been slowed by the foot-dragging of entrenched monopolies."
Business long-distance revenue rose $223 million to $5.6 billion in the quarter, up 4.1 percent from a year ago, driven by strong double-digit growth in data services.
Revenue from consumer long-distance services declined $50 million to $6 billion in the quarter, down less than 1 percent, with volume growth slightly below the industry rate.

New programmes that offer free minutes to customers reduced the revenue growth rate by about 1.6 percent. As a result of aggressive promotional pricing, international volumes had double-digit growth, while revenue declined slightly.
At the end of the quarter, AT&T had 7.6 million cellular telephone subscribers, up 23 percent from a year earlier.
The AT&T Worldnet Internet access service ended the quarter with a subscriber base of about 923,000.
